lessons.title: Lesson 1: What the Internet of Things is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain IoT and spot IoT devices around you.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples from home, work and the field, you will identify IoT devices and explain the value and the risk of each, naming at least three devices correctly.
The Internet of Things (IoT) means physical things that sense the world, connect to a network and share data, often with no person typing anything. A smart thermostat measures the room and turns the heat on. A fitness tracker counts steps and sends them to your phone.
IoT is used at home (doorbell cameras, smart plugs, voice speakers), at work (machines that report when they need repair, called predictive maintenance), in logistics (GPS trackers on trucks and containers), in farming (soil moisture sensors), in health (heart-rate monitors) and in cities (smart traffic lights).
The value is in what the data lets you do: catch a problem early, save energy, or act from far away. The risk is that every connected device is one more thing that can be hacked or can leak private data, so security is part of every IoT job.
Words to know:
- Internet of Things (IoT): physical objects with sensors and a network connection that share data.
- Smart device: an everyday object that can connect and act on data.
- Predictive maintenance: using sensor data to fix a machine before it breaks.
Try it now: Walk through your home, workplace or a store and list five connected devices you see or use. For each one, write what it senses and what it does with the data.
You can now explain what IoT is and name IoT devices in daily life and at work.

check.q: What makes a device part of the Internet of Things?
options: It costs more than a regular device
It senses something, connects to a network and shares data
It only works with a keyboard
check.why: IoT devices sense the world, connect and share data, often with no person typing.

check.q: Your unit's motor pool wants trucks to report problems before they break down. What is this use of IoT called?
check.why: Machines reporting when they need repair before they fail is predictive maintenance.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The four layers: sensors, devices, connection and cloud
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Trace the data in an IoT system from the sensor to the action.
This lesson builds toward: Given an IoT project such as a freezer alarm, you will trace the data from the sensor through the device and connection to the cloud and the action, naming all four layers in the right order.
Most IoT systems have four layers. 1) Sensors measure something: temperature, motion, light, location, moisture. 2) A device (often a small, cheap computer called a microcontroller, like an ESP32 or Arduino) reads the sensor and sends the data. 3) A connection carries the data: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular or a long-range radio. 4) A cloud service or app stores the data, shows it on a dashboard and sends alerts.
Some devices also have actuators: parts that do something in the real world, such as a motor that opens a valve, a relay that switches on a fan, or a buzzer.
Sometimes the device makes the decision itself instead of waiting for the cloud. This is edge computing. It is faster, keeps working when the internet is down, and sends less data.
Step by step:
- Name what is measured (the sensor).
- Name the device that reads it.
- Name how the data travels (the connection).
- Name where it goes and who sees it (cloud, app, dashboard).
- Name the action, by a person or an actuator.
Words to know:
- Sensor: a part that measures something in the real world.
- Microcontroller: a tiny, low-cost computer on a chip that runs one program.
- Actuator: a part that acts in the real world, like a motor, relay or buzzer.
- Dashboard: a screen that shows live data in charts and numbers.
- Edge computing: processing data on or near the device instead of in the cloud.
Try it now: Pick one device from your list in Lesson 1. Draw boxes for its four layers (sensor, device, connection, cloud or app) with arrows between them, and add the action at the end.
You can now trace data through the four layers of an IoT system and name sensors and actuators.

check.q: In an IoT system, what is a microcontroller's job?
options: To store data in the cloud
To read the sensor and send the data
check.why: The device, often a microcontroller, reads the sensor and sends the data on.

check.q: A remote gate sensor must keep working when the internet goes down. What design helps?
options: Send every reading to the cloud first
Let the device make the decision itself (edge computing)
check.why: Edge computing lets the device decide on its own, so it keeps working without the internet.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How devices connect and talk
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a suitable connection for an IoT device.
This lesson builds toward: Given where a device sits, its power and how much data it sends, you will choose a suitable connection and explain how a protocol like MQTT carries its messages, with a reason that fits range, power and data.
There is no single best connection; each trades off range, power and data. Wi-Fi is fast and common at home and work, but uses a lot of power. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) uses very little power and has short range, good for wearables and phones. Cellular (4G, 5G and low-power versions) works almost anywhere with a signal, good for vehicles and remote sites, but needs a data plan. LoRaWAN is a low-power, long-range radio for small amounts of data, used for farm and city sensors.
Devices also need a shared language, called a protocol, to send messages. MQTT is a popular light protocol: a device publishes a reading to a topic, such as pantry/freezer/temp, and any app subscribed to that topic receives it. HTTP, the same protocol websites use, is also common.
Battery devices save power by sleeping most of the time and waking up only to read and send.
Step by step:
- How far must the data travel?
- Is there power, or only a battery?
- How much data, and how often?
- Is there Wi-Fi or cell signal where it will sit?
- Pick the connection that fits all four answers.
Words to know:
- Wi-Fi: fast wireless networking for homes and offices; uses more power.
- Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE): very low-power, short-range wireless.
- Cellular: connection through mobile phone networks.
- LoRaWAN: a long-range, low-power radio network for small amounts of data.
- Protocol: an agreed set of rules for sending messages.
- MQTT: a light messaging protocol where devices publish to topics and apps subscribe.
Try it now: Choose the best connection for each and write one reason: a step counter on your wrist, a soil sensor in a field 5 km from any building, a GPS tracker on a delivery truck, and a smart plug in a living room.
You can now pick a suitable connection and explain how IoT devices send messages.

options: A light protocol where devices publish readings to topics
check.why: MQTT is a light protocol: devices publish to a topic and subscribed apps receive it.

check.q: A battery sensor in a storage yard with no Wi-Fi sends one small reading an hour. What do you pick?
check.why: LoRaWAN is low-power and long-range for small amounts of data.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: From reading to action: writing an alert rule
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a simple rule in Python that turns a sensor reading into an alert.
This lesson builds toward: Given a sensor reading and a safe range, you will write an alert rule as a Python if-statement that avoids false alarms, so the rule gives the right result for test readings.
The heart of most IoT projects is a rule: if a reading crosses a limit, do something. If the pantry freezer is warmer than -15 degrees C for 10 minutes, text the manager. If the soil moisture drops below 30 percent, open the water valve.
In Python, a rule is an if-statement. For example: temp = 28.5, then if temp > 27: print("ALERT: server closet too hot") else: print("OK"). On a real device the reading comes from the sensor, and the action might light an LED, switch a relay or send a message.
Good rules avoid false alarms. One spike might be a door opening for a moment, so many systems wait for several readings in a row before alerting. Pick a limit with the people who know the equipment, and decide who gets the alert and what they should do.
Step by step:
- Decide what you measure and its safe range.
- Pick the limit that means trouble.
- Write it as if reading > limit: (or < limit).
- Decide the action: a message, a light or a relay.
- Add a rule to avoid false alarms, like several readings in a row.
Words to know:
- Rule: an if-then instruction: if this happens, do that.
- Threshold: the limit that triggers an action.
- False alarm: an alert when nothing is really wrong.
- Reading: one measurement from a sensor.
Try it now: Open Google Colab (colab.research.google.com) or any Python editor. Make a list of six temperature readings, such as [22, 23, 29, 30, 31, 24]. Loop through them and print "ALERT" for any reading over 27 and "OK" for the rest. Bonus: only alert when two readings in a row are over 27.
You can now write a simple alert rule in Python that turns sensor readings into an action.

check.q: The rule is: if temp > 27: print("ALERT"). The reading is 25. What prints?
check.why: 25 is not greater than 27, so the if-statement does not run.

check.q: A server closet alarm fires every time the door opens for a second. What do you change?
options: Turn the alarm off for good
Alert only after several high readings in a row
check.why: Waiting for several readings in a row stops false alarms from short spikes.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Trying a simulated device in your browser
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Run a simulated microcontroller with a sensor and see readings change.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free online simulator, you will run a simulated microcontroller with a temperature sensor and test your alert rule, seeing the alert fire when you change the reading.
You can practice IoT without buying parts. An online simulator such as Wokwi lets you place a virtual board like an ESP32, add a sensor like a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor, and run code in your web browser. Check the site for which features are free and whether you need an account.
The easiest start is to open one of the simulator's ready-made example projects for the ESP32 with a DHT22, then read the code and run it. In MicroPython, a version of Python for small devices, the key lines look like this: sensor = dht.DHT22(machine.Pin(15)), then sensor.measure() and t = sensor.temperature(). The pin number must match the pin the sensor is wired to in the diagram.
While the simulation runs you can click the virtual sensor and change its temperature, then watch your printed readings and your alert rule respond. That is exactly how you test a real device before installing it.
Step by step:
- Open the simulator website in your browser.
- Find an example project for an ESP32 with a DHT22 sensor.
- Read the code: find where it reads the sensor and where it prints.
- Start the simulation and watch the readings.
- Change the virtual sensor's temperature and add your alert rule from Lesson 4.
Words to know:
- Simulator: software that acts like real hardware so you can test without buying it.
- ESP32: a low-cost microcontroller with built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
- DHT22: a common, low-cost temperature and humidity sensor.
- MicroPython: a small version of Python that runs on microcontrollers.
- Pin: a metal connection point on a board where parts are wired.
Official sources:
- Wokwi online electronics simulator
Try it now: Open an ESP32 and DHT22 example in an online simulator and run it. Change the virtual sensor's temperature at least twice and write down the readings. If you can, add an if-statement that prints "ALERT" above 27 degrees C. If you cannot use the simulator, trace the example code on paper: mark the line that reads the sensor and the line that prints.
You can now run and test a simulated IoT device and connect its readings to an alert rule.

check.q: In MicroPython, which line reads the temperature after sensor.measure()?
check.why: sensor.temperature() returns the reading after sensor.measure().

check.q: Your simulated alert rule never fires. How do you test it?
options: Click the virtual sensor and raise its temperature above the limit
Delete the code and start over
Change the pin number at random
check.why: Changing the virtual sensor's reading lets you watch the rule respond.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Securing IoT devices and planning your project
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Apply the key security steps to connected devices and finish your project plan.
This lesson builds toward: For every connected device in your plan, you will list the steps that keep the devices secure, with at least five correct steps.
Connected devices are a favorite target for attackers because many ship with weak default passwords and are never updated. A hacked camera or smart plug can spy on people or be used to attack others.
The US Federal Trade Commission's advice for home devices: change the default username and password and do not reuse passwords; turn on two-factor authentication where offered; keep firmware and the companion app updated; turn off features you do not use, such as remote management; and disconnect old devices. For the router: change its default settings, turn on encryption and check for updates. A guest network keeps smart devices apart from computers with private files.
At work, also keep a list of every connected device, put IoT devices on their own network, and only collect the data you need, especially when cameras or microphones are involved. Ask the organization's IT or security team before connecting anything to a work network.
Step by step:
- Change every default password; use a unique, strong one.
- Turn on two-factor authentication where it is offered.
- Update firmware and companion apps.
- Turn off features you do not use; disconnect old devices.
- Put smart devices on a separate or guest network, and keep a device list.
Words to know:
- Default password: the password a device ships with; attackers know these lists.
- Firmware: the built-in software that runs a device.
- Two-factor authentication: signing in with a password plus a second proof, like a code.
- Guest network: a separate Wi-Fi network that keeps devices away from your main computers.
- Device inventory: a list of every connected device you are responsible for.
Official sources:
- FTC Consumer Advice: Securing Your Internet-Connected Devices at Home
- CISA: Secure Our World
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page IoT plan (for example a server closet, food pantry freezer or garden). Name the sensor, device, connection and where the data goes, draw the flow from sensor to alert, write the alert rule as a Python if-statement, and list five security steps you will take.
You can now secure connected devices and plan a complete IoT monitoring project.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Parts of the system The sensor, device or destination is missing. Names the sensor, the device, the connection and where the data goes. Also names an actuator or an edge decision and says why it helps. Data flow drawing No drawing, or the steps are out of order. The drawing shows sensor, device, connection, cloud or app, and alert in order. The drawing also shows who gets the alert and what they do. Connection choice The connection does not fit the place or power, such as Wi-Fi in a field with no Wi-Fi. The connection fits the range, power and data of the project. Explains why one other connection would not fit as well. Alert rule The rule is missing or would not work, such as a wrong comparison. A correct Python if-statement with a sensible limit and action. Also avoids false alarms, such as waiting for several readings, and was tested in the simulator. Security steps Fewer than five steps, or steps that do not protect the devices. Five correct steps, such as unique passwords, updates and a separate network. Also includes a device list and asking IT before connecting at work. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why are IoT devices a common target for attackers?
options: Many ship with weak default passwords and are never updated
check.why: Weak default passwords and missing updates make many devices easy to break into.

check.q: A new door camera has a remote management feature you will not use. What do you do?
options: Share its password with the team
Reuse your email password on it
check.why: Turning off features you do not use removes ways in for attackers.
